newsitem.title: Afghanistan: Kabul bombed by ousted Afghan government forces.
newsitem.headline: Kabul bombed by ousted Afghan government forces.

text.p: Forces loyal to the ousted Afghan government bombed Kabul and launched a blistering assault on Taleban troops north of the capital on Thursday, breaking a two-day lull in Afghanistan's latest war.
Witnesses said the two air raids killed three children and wounded seven -- the first war-related civilian deaths in Kabul since the purist Islamic Taleban militia took over the capital a month ago.
The five bombs were apparently aimed at the airport, used for both military and civilian traffic, on the northeastern fringe of the city. The airport, however, appeared undamaged, the witnesses said.
One bomb hit a mountainside next to the airport. Two more hit a field about 400 metres (yards) from the airport. One, the size of a man, did not explode.

Two bombs landed in Deh Kepaklo, in the northwest area of Kabul. A fourth bomb did explode, but it was not immediately clear where it hit in the midst of heavy anti-aircraft fire sent up by the Taleban defenders of the capital.
The Taleban militia fired one ground-to-air missile, but it did not appear to hit any of the planes, believed to belong to northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum.

The anti-Taleban northern alliance between Dostum's forces and fighters under Ahmad Shah Masood launched a fierce assault around the strategic De Sabz pass, 30 km (20 miles) north of Kabul, Reuters correspondent Chris Bird reported.
"God willing we will take the pass today," said Niq Mohammad, a commander with forces under Masood, the government military chief driven from Kabul a month ago.
The commander said the attack, a pincer movement to support Dostum's forces, began around 6 am (0130 gmt).
Thursday's air raids, about an hour apart, and assault on the De Sabz pass followed an apparently successful attack on Wednesday afternoon by Masood's forces, reliable sources said.
They said Masood appeared to have broken a 10-day stalemate in fighting over a range of hills across the plain 25-30 km (15-19 miles) north of Kabul.
They said he sent a strong force down the western side of the valley around the flank of the Taleban lines, then swung east to take the village of Morad Beg, some 13 km (eight miles) from Kabul.

There was no immediate confirmation of the report because Taleban fighters manning a checkpoint at the top of the five km (three-mile) pass leading out of Kabul have refused to allow Western reporters through for the past week.
Morad Beg is the last major village on the main road running down the valley into Kabul. Between the village and the city is a stretch of gently undulating plain with few inhabitants.
The Taleban have stationed tanks, artillery and multiple rocket launchers along that stretch of road.

The sources said Masood's aim appeared to be to get behind the Taleban lines in the hills which have frustrated repeated attempts by Masood and Dostum to break through on the eastern side of the valley.
